title: Book 8, Chapter 26 — Twenty-first Year of the War—Recall of Alcibiades to Samos—Revolt of Euboea and Downfall of the Four Hundred—Battle of Cynossema
paragraphs: In the same summer, immediately after this, the Peloponnesians, having refused to fight with their fleet united because they did not consider themselves a match for the enemy, and being at a loss where to find money for so many ships — especially as Tissaphernes had proven such a bad paymaster — sent off Clearchus, son of Ramphias, with forty ships to Pharnabazus, in keeping with the original instructions from the Peloponnese. Pharnabazus had invited them and was prepared to provide pay, and Byzantium had also sent offers to revolt to them. These Peloponnesian ships accordingly put out into the open sea, in order to escape the notice of the Athenians. Overtaken by a storm, the majority of them with Clearchus put in at Delos, and afterwards returned to Miletus, where Clearchus continued by land to the Hellespont to take up his command. Ten of their number, however, under the Megarian Helixus, made it through to the Hellespont and brought about the revolt of Byzantium. After this the commanders at Samos were informed of it, and sent a squadron against them to guard the Hellespont. An engagement took place before Byzantium between eight vessels on each side.

Meanwhile the chiefs at Samos, and especially Thrasybulus, who from the moment he had changed the government had been firmly resolved to recall Alcibiades, at last in an assembly brought over the mass of the soldiery. On their voting for his recall and amnesty, he sailed over to Tissaphernes and brought Alcibiades to Samos, being convinced that their only chance of salvation lay in his bringing Tissaphernes over from the Peloponnesians to themselves. An assembly was then held in which Alcibiades complained of and lamented his private misfortune in having been banished. Speaking at great length about public affairs, he raised their hopes for the future and extravagantly magnified his own influence with Tissaphernes. His aim was to make the oligarchical government at Athens afraid of him, to hasten the dissolution of the clubs, to increase his credit with the army at Samos and heighten their own confidence, and finally to prejudice the enemy as strongly as possible against Tissaphernes and blast the hopes they had of him. Alcibiades accordingly held out to the army such extravagant promises as the following: that Tissaphernes had solemnly assured him that, if he could only trust the Athenians, they should never want for supplies while he had anything left, no — not even if he should have to coin his own silver couch — and that he would bring the Phoenician fleet now at Aspendus to the Athenians instead of to the Peloponnesians; but that he could only trust the Athenians if Alcibiades were recalled and made his security for them.

On hearing this and much more besides, the Athenians at once elected him general along with the others, and put all their affairs into his hands. There was now not a man in the army who would have exchanged his present hopes of safety and vengeance on the Four Hundred for any consideration whatever. After what they had been told, they were now inclined to disdain the enemy in front of them and to sail at once for Piraeus. To the plan of sailing for Piraeus, leaving their more immediate enemies behind, Alcibiades opposed the most positive refusal, in spite of the numbers who insisted on it, saying that, now that he had been elected general, he would first sail to Tissaphernes and concert with him measures for carrying on the war. Accordingly, on leaving this assembly, he immediately took his departure, in order to make it appear that there was complete confidence between them, and also wishing to increase his standing with Tissaphernes and to show that he had now been elected general and was in a position to do him good or evil as he chose — thus managing to frighten the Athenians with Tissaphernes and Tissaphernes with the Athenians.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesians at Miletus heard of the recall of Alcibiades, and being already distrustful of Tissaphernes, now became far more disgusted with him than ever. Indeed, after their refusal to go out and give battle to the Athenians when they appeared before Miletus, Tissaphernes had grown slacker than ever in his payments, and even before that, on Alcibiades' account, his unpopularity had been on the increase. Gathering together, just as before, the soldiers and some persons of standing besides the soldiery began to reckon up that they had never yet received their pay in full, that what they did receive was small, and even that paid irregularly, and that unless they fought a decisive battle or moved to some station where they could get supplies, the ships' crews would desert. They blamed Astyochus, who humored Tissaphernes for his own private advantage.

The army was engaged in these reflections when the following disturbance occurred concerning Astyochus. Most of the Syracusan and Thurian sailors were freemen, and these, the freest crews in the armament, were also the boldest in setting on Astyochus and demanding their pay. He answered somewhat stiffly and threatened them, and when Dorieus spoke up for his own sailors, he even went so far as to lift his baton against him. Seeing this, the mass of the men, in sailor fashion, rushed in fury to strike Astyochus. He, however, saw them in time and fled for refuge to an altar, and so they were parted without his being struck. Meanwhile the fort built by Tissaphernes in Miletus was surprised and taken by the Milesians, and the garrison turned out — an act which met with the approval of the rest of the allies, and especially of the Syracusans, but found no favor with Lichas, who said moreover that the Milesians and the rest in the King's country ought to show reasonable submission to Tissaphernes and to court him, until the war should be happily settled. The Milesians were angry with him for this and other things of the kind, and when he afterwards died of sickness, would not allow him to be buried where the Lacedaemonians with the army wished.

The army's discontent with Astyochus and Tissaphernes had reached this pitch when Mindarus arrived from Lacedaemon to succeed Astyochus as admiral and took up the command. Astyochus now set sail for home, and Tissaphernes sent with him one of his confidants, Gaulites, a Carian who spoke both languages, to complain of the Milesians for the affair of the fort, and at the same time to defend himself against the Milesians, who were, as he was aware, on their way to Sparta chiefly to denounce his conduct, and had with them Hermocrates, who was to accuse Tissaphernes of joining with Alcibiades to ruin the Peloponnesian cause and of playing a double game. Indeed, Hermocrates had always been at odds with him about the pay not being restored in full. Eventually, when Hermocrates was banished from Syracuse, and new commanders — Potamis, Myscon, and Demarchus — had come out to Miletus to the ships of the Syracusans, Tissaphernes pressed harder than ever upon him in his exile, and among other charges accused him of having once asked him for money, and then, when he failed to obtain it, declaring himself his enemy.

While Astyochus and the Milesians and Hermocrates were sailing for Lacedaemon, Alcibiades had now crossed back from Tissaphernes to Samos. After his return, the envoys of the Four Hundred, sent, as has been mentioned above, to pacify and explain matters to the forces at Samos, arrived from Delos. An assembly was held in which they tried to speak. The soldiers at first would not hear them, and cried out to put to death the subverters of the democracy, but at last, after some difficulty, calmed down and gave them a hearing. The envoys then proceeded to inform them that the recent change had been made to save the city, not to ruin it or to deliver it over to the enemy — for they had already had an opportunity of doing this when the enemy invaded the country during their government. They claimed that all the Five Thousand would have their proper share in the government, and that their hearers' relatives had suffered no outrage, as Chaereas had slanderously reported, nor any other ill treatment, but were all in undisturbed enjoyment of their property, just as they had left them. Besides these, they made a number of other statements which had no better success with their angry audience. Amid a host of different opinions, the one which found most favor was sailing to Piraeus. Now it was that Alcibiades for the first time did the state a service, and one of the most signal kind. For when the Athenians at Samos were bent on sailing against their countrymen — in which case Ionia and the Hellespont would most certainly at once have passed into the enemy's hands — Alcibiades was the one who prevented them. At that moment, when no other man would have been able to hold back the multitude, he put a stop to the intended expedition and rebuked and turned aside the resentment felt, on personal grounds, against the envoys. He dismissed them with an answer from himself, to the effect that he did not object to the government of the Five Thousand, but insisted that the Four Hundred be deposed and the Council of Five Hundred reinstated in power; meanwhile any retrenchments for economy, by which pay might be better found for the armament, met with his entire approval. In general he urged them to hold out and show a bold face to the enemy, since if the city were saved, there was good hope that the two parties might some day be reconciled, whereas if either were once destroyed — the one at Samos or the one at Athens — there would no longer be anyone left to be reconciled to. Meanwhile envoys arrived from the Argives, with offers of support to the Athenian commons at Samos. Alcibiades thanked them and dismissed them with a request to come when called upon. The Argives were accompanied by the crew of the Paralus, whom we left placed in a troopship by the Four Hundred with orders to cruise round Euboea, and who, being employed to carry to Lacedaemon some Athenian envoys sent by the Four Hundred — Laespodias, Aristophon, and Melesias — as they sailed past Argos laid hands on the envoys, and delivering them over to the Argives as the chief subverters of the democracy, themselves, instead of returning to Athens, took the Argive envoys on board and came to Samos in the galley that had been entrusted to them.

The same summer, at the time when the return of Alcibiades, coupled with the general conduct of Tissaphernes, had carried the Peloponnesians' discontent to its height — for they no longer entertained any doubt that he had joined the Athenians — Tissaphernes, wishing, it would seem, to clear himself with them of these charges, prepared to go after the Phoenician fleet to Aspendus, and invited Lichas to go with him. He said that he would appoint Tamos as his lieutenant to provide pay for the armament during his absence. Accounts differ, and it is not easy to determine with what intention he went to Aspendus and did not bring the fleet after all. That one hundred and forty-seven Phoenician ships came as far as Aspendus is certain, but why they did not come on has been variously accounted for. Some think he went away in pursuit of his plan of wasting Peloponnesian resources, since at any rate Tamos, his lieutenant, far from being any better, proved a worse paymaster than himself. Others think he brought the Phoenicians to Aspendus to extract money from them for their discharge, never having intended to employ them. Others again say it was in view of the outcry against him at Lacedaemon, so that it could be said he was not at fault, but that the ships were really manned and that he had certainly gone to fetch them. To my own mind it seems only too clear that he did not bring up the fleet because he wished to wear out and paralyze the Hellenic forces — that is, to waste their strength by the time lost during his journey to Aspendus, and to keep them evenly balanced by not throwing his weight onto either side of the scale. Had he wished to finish the war, he could have done so, assuming of course that he had appeared in such a way as to leave no room for doubt; for by bringing up the fleet he would in all probability have given the victory to the Lacedaemonians, whose navy, even as it was, faced the Athenian more as an equal than as an inferior. But what convicts him most clearly is the excuse he put forward for not bringing the ships. He said that the number assembled was less than the King had ordered. Surely it would only have enhanced his credit if he had spent little of the King's money and achieved the same end at less cost. In any case, whatever his intention, Tissaphernes went to Aspendus and saw the Phoenicians, and the Peloponnesians at his request sent a Lacedaemonian called Philip with two galleys to fetch the fleet.

Alcibiades, finding that Tissaphernes had gone to Aspendus, himself sailed there with thirteen ships, promising to do a great and certain service to the Athenians at Samos, since he would either bring the Phoenician fleet to the Athenians, or at any rate prevent its joining the Peloponnesians. In all probability he had long known that Tissaphernes never meant to bring the fleet at all, and wished to compromise him as much as possible in the eyes of the Peloponnesians by his apparent friendship for himself and the Athenians, and so in a sense to oblige him to join their side.

While Alcibiades weighed anchor and sailed eastward straight for Phaselis and Caunus, the envoys sent by the Four Hundred to Samos arrived at Athens. On their delivering the message from Alcibiades, telling them to hold out and show a firm front to the enemy, and saying that he had great hopes of reconciling them with the army and of overcoming the Peloponnesians, the majority of the members of the oligarchy — already discontented and only too inclined to be quit of the business in any safe way they could — were at once greatly strengthened in their resolve. These now banded together and strongly criticized the administration. Their leaders were some of the principal generals and men in office under the oligarchy, such as Theramenes, son of Hagnon, Aristocrates, son of Scellias, and others. Although among the most prominent members of the government, they argued — being afraid, as they said, of the army at Samos, and most especially of Alcibiades, and also lest the envoys whom they had sent to Lacedaemon might do the state some harm without the authority of the people — without insisting on objections to the excessive concentration of power in a few hands, that the Five Thousand must be shown to exist not merely in name but in reality, and the constitution placed on a fairer basis. But this was merely their political slogan. Most of them were driven by private ambition into the line of conduct so surely fatal to oligarchies that arise out of democracies. For all at once each of them pretends to be not just an equal but the chief and master of his fellows, while under a democracy a disappointed candidate accepts his defeat more easily, since he has not the humiliation of being beaten by his equals. But what most clearly encouraged the malcontents was the power of Alcibiades at Samos, and their own disbelief in the stability of the oligarchy. It was now a race between them as to which should first become the leader of the commons.

Meanwhile the leaders and members of the Four Hundred most opposed to a democratic form of government — Phrynichus, who had quarreled with Alcibiades during his command at Samos, Aristarchus, the bitter and inveterate enemy of the commons, and Pisander and Antiphon and others of the chiefs who already, as soon as they entered upon power, and again when the army at Samos seceded from them and declared for a democracy, had sent envoys from their own body to Lacedaemon and made every effort for peace, and had built the wall in Eetionia — now redoubled their exertions when their envoys returned from Samos and they saw not only the people but their own most trusted associates turning against them. Alarmed at the state of things at Athens as at Samos, they now hastily sent off Antiphon and Phrynichus and ten others, with instructions to make peace with Lacedaemon on any terms whatever, no matter what, that should be at all tolerable. Meanwhile they pressed on more actively than ever with the wall in Eetionia. Now the meaning of this wall, according to Theramenes and his supporters, was not so much to keep out the army of Samos, in case it tried to force its way into Piraeus, as to be able to let in, at pleasure, the fleet and army of the enemy. For Eetionia is a mole of Piraeus, close to the entrance of the harbor, and was now fortified in connection with the wall already existing on the land side, so that a few men placed in it could command the entrance — the old wall on the land side and the new one now being built within on the side of the sea, both ending in one of the two towers standing at the narrow mouth of the harbor. They also walled off the largest porch in Piraeus, which was directly connected with this wall, and kept it in their own hands, forcing everyone to unload there the corn that came into the harbor and what they had in stock, and to take it out from there when they sold it.

These measures had long provoked Theramenes' protests, and when the envoys returned from Lacedaemon without having effected any general pacification, he declared that this wall was likely to prove the ruin of the state. At this moment forty-two ships from the Peloponnese, including some Siceliot and Italiot vessels from Locri and Tarentum, had been invited over by the Euboeans, and were already lying off Las in Laconia preparing for the voyage to Euboea, under the command of Agesandridas, son of Agesander, a Spartan. Theramenes now declared that this squadron was destined not so much to aid Euboea as to aid the party fortifying Eetionia, and that unless precautions were quickly taken, the city would be surprised and lost. This was no mere slander, since some such plan really was being entertained by those he accused. Their first wish was to have the oligarchy without giving up the empire; failing this, to keep their ships and walls and remain independent; and if this too were denied them, sooner than be the first victims of the restored democracy, they were resolved to call in the enemy and make peace, give up their walls and ships, and at all costs retain possession of the government, if their own lives were only assured to them.

For this reason they pushed forward the construction of their work with posterns and entrances and means of letting in the enemy, eager to have it finished in time. Meanwhile the murmurs against them were at first confined to a few persons and went on in secret, until Phrynichus, after his return from the embassy to Lacedaemon, was waylaid and stabbed in the open marketplace by one of the Peripoli, falling down dead before he had gone far from the council chamber. The assassin escaped, but his accomplice, an Argive, was caught and put to the torture by the Four Hundred, without their being able to extract from him the name of his employer, or anything more than that he knew of many men who used to assemble at the house of the commander of the Peripoli and at other houses. There the matter was allowed to drop. This so emboldened Theramenes and Aristocrates and the rest of their partisans in the Four Hundred and outside, that they now decided to act. For by this time the ships had sailed round from Las, and anchoring at Epidaurus had overrun Aegina. Theramenes asserted that, being bound for Euboea, they would never have sailed in to Aegina and come back to anchor at Epidaurus, unless they had been invited to come and aid in the designs of which he had always accused the government. Further inaction had therefore now become impossible. In the end, after a great many seditious speeches and suspicions, they set to work in real earnest. The heavy infantry in Piraeus building the wall in Eetionia — among whom was Aristocrates, a colonel, with his own tribe — laid hands on Alexicles, a general under the oligarchy and a devoted adherent of the cabal, and took him into a house and kept him there. They were assisted by one Hermon, commander of the Peripoli in Munychia, and others, and above all had with them the great bulk of the heavy infantry. As soon as the news reached the Four Hundred, who happened to be sitting in the council chamber, all except the disaffected wished at once to go to the posts where the arms were, and threatened Theramenes and his party. Theramenes defended himself, and said he was ready immediately to go and help to rescue Alexicles. Taking with him one of the generals belonging to his party, he went down to Piraeus, followed by Aristarchus and some young men of the cavalry. All was now panic and confusion. Those in the city imagined that Piraeus was already taken and the prisoner put to death, while those in Piraeus expected at any moment to be attacked by the party in the city. The older men, however, stopped the persons running up and down the town and making for the stands of arms, and Thucydides the Pharsalian, proxenus of the city, came forward and threw himself in the way of the rival factions, appealing to them not to ruin the state while the enemy was still at hand waiting for his opportunity. He at length succeeded in quieting them and in keeping their hands off each other. Meanwhile Theramenes came down to Piraeus, being himself one of the generals, and raged and stormed at the heavy infantry, while Aristarchus and the adversaries of the people were angry in earnest. Most of the heavy infantry, however, went on with the work without faltering, and asked Theramenes if he thought the wall had been built for any good purpose, and whether it would not be better to pull it down. To this he answered that, if they thought it best to pull it down, he for his part agreed with them. On this the heavy infantry and a number of the people in Piraeus immediately got up onto the fortification and began to demolish it. Now their cry to the multitude was that all should join in the work who wished the Five Thousand to govern instead of the Four Hundred. For instead of saying in so many words "all who want the commons to govern," they still disguised themselves under the name of the Five Thousand, being afraid that these might really exist, and that they might be speaking to one of their number and get into trouble through ignorance. Indeed this was why the Four Hundred neither wished the Five Thousand to exist nor to have it known that they did not exist, holding the view that to give themselves so many partners in empire would be downright democracy, while the mystery in question would make the people afraid of one another.

The next day the Four Hundred, although alarmed, nevertheless assembled in the council chamber, while the heavy infantry in Piraeus, after releasing their prisoner Alexicles and pulling down the fortification, went with their arms to the theatre of Dionysus, close to Munychia, and there held an assembly in which they decided to march into the city, and setting forth accordingly halted in the Anaceum. Here they were joined by some delegates from the Four Hundred, who reasoned with them one by one and persuaded those whom they saw to be the most moderate to remain quiet themselves and to keep the rest in check. They said they would make known the Five Thousand and have the Four Hundred chosen from them in rotation, as the Five Thousand should decide, and meanwhile begged them not to ruin the state or drive it into the arms of the enemy. After a great many had spoken and been spoken to, the whole body of heavy infantry became calmer than before, absorbed by their fears for the country at large, and now agreed to hold an assembly on a fixed day in the theatre of Dionysus for the restoration of concord.

When the day came for the assembly in the theatre, and they were about to assemble, news arrived that the forty-two ships under Agesandridas were sailing from Megara along the coast of Salamis. Every man now thought that this was just what Theramenes and his party had so often said — that the ships were sailing to the fortification — and concluded that they had done well to demolish it. But though it may have been by appointment that Agesandridas was hovering about Epidaurus and the neighborhood, he would also naturally have been kept there by the hope of an opportunity arising out of the troubles in the city. In any case the Athenians, on receipt of the news, immediately ran down in mass to Piraeus, seeing themselves threatened by the enemy with a worse war than their war among themselves — not at a distance, but close to the harbor of Athens. Some went on board the ships already afloat, while others launched fresh vessels, or ran to defend the walls and the mouth of the harbor.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesian vessels sailed by, and rounding Sunium anchored between Thoricus and Prasiae, and afterwards arrived at Oropus. The Athenians, with revolution in the city and unwilling to lose a moment in going to the relief of their most important possession — for Euboea was everything to them now that they were shut out of Attica — were forced to put to sea in haste with untrained crews, and sent Thymochares with some vessels to Eretria. These on their arrival, with the ships already in Euboea, made up a total of thirty-six vessels, and were immediately forced to engage. For Agesandridas, after his crews had dined, put out from Oropus, which is about seven miles from Eretria by sea. The Athenians, seeing him sailing up, immediately began to man their vessels. The sailors, however, instead of being by their ships as they supposed, had gone away to buy provisions for their dinner in the houses on the outskirts of the town. The Eretrians had so arranged that there should be nothing on sale in the marketplace, in order that the Athenians might be a long time in manning their ships, and, the enemy's attack taking them by surprise, might be forced to put to sea just as they were. A signal was also raised in Eretria to give them notice in Oropus when to put to sea. The Athenians, forced to put out so poorly prepared, engaged off the harbor of Eretria, and after holding their own for some little while in spite of all this, were at length put to flight and chased to the shore. Those who took refuge in Eretria, which they presumed friendly to them, met their fate in that city, being butchered by the inhabitants. Those who fled to the Athenian fort in Eretrian territory, and the vessels that got to Chalcis, were saved. The Peloponnesians, after taking twenty-two Athenian ships and killing or capturing the crews, set up a trophy, and not long afterwards effected the revolt of the whole of Euboea (except Oreus, which was held by the Athenians themselves), and made a general settlement of the affairs of the island.

When the news of what had happened in Euboea reached Athens, a panic ensued such as they had never before known. Neither the disaster in Sicily, great as it had seemed at the time, nor any other had ever so alarmed them. The camp at Samos was in revolt; they had no more ships, or men to man them; they were at odds among themselves and might at any moment come to blows. A disaster of this magnitude, on top of all the rest — by which they had lost their fleet, and worst of all, Euboea, which was of more value to them than Attica — could not occur without throwing them into the deepest despondency. Meanwhile their greatest and most immediate fear was the possibility that the enemy, emboldened by his victory, might come straight at them and sail against Piraeus, which they no longer had ships to defend. Every moment they expected him to arrive. With a little more courage, he could easily have done so, in which case he would either have aggravated the dissensions in the city by his presence, or, if he had stayed to besiege it, would have forced the fleet from Ionia, although the enemy of the oligarchy, to come to the rescue of their country and their relatives. Meanwhile he would have made himself master of the Hellespont, Ionia, the islands, and everything as far as Euboea — in a word, of the whole Athenian empire. But here, as on so many other occasions, the Lacedaemonians proved the most convenient people in the world for the Athenians to be at war with. The wide difference between the two characters — the slowness and lack of energy of the Lacedaemonians, as contrasted with the dash and enterprise of their opponents — was of the greatest service, especially to a maritime empire like Athens. This was shown by the Syracusans, who were most like the Athenians in character, and also most successful in fighting them.

Nevertheless, on receipt of the news, the Athenians manned twenty ships and called immediately a first assembly in the Pnyx, where they had been used to meet formerly. They deposed the Four Hundred and voted to hand over the government to the Five Thousand, of which body all who furnished a suit of armor were to be members. They also decreed that no one should receive pay for the discharge of any office, or if he did, should be held accursed. Many other assemblies were held afterwards, in which lawmakers were elected and all other measures taken to form a constitution. It was during the first period of this constitution that the Athenians appear to have enjoyed the best government they ever had, at least in my time. The fusion of the high and the low was carried out with judgment, and this was what first enabled the state to lift its head after its many disasters. They also voted for the recall of Alcibiades and other exiles, and sent to him and to the camp at Samos, urging them to devote themselves vigorously to the war.

On this revolution taking place, the party of Pisander and Alexicles and the chiefs of the oligarchs immediately withdrew to Decelea, with the single exception of Aristarchus, one of the generals, who hastily took some of the most barbarian of the archers and marched to Oenoe. This was an Athenian fort on the Boeotian border, at that moment besieged by the Corinthians, who were irritated by the loss of a party returning from Decelea that had been cut off by the garrison. The Corinthians had volunteered for this service and had called on the Boeotians to assist them. After communicating with them, Aristarchus deceived the garrison in Oenoe by telling them that their countrymen in the city had come to terms with the Lacedaemonians, and that one of the conditions of the surrender was that they must hand the place over to the Boeotians. The garrison believed him, since he was a general, and besides knew nothing of what had occurred owing to the siege, and so they evacuated the fort under truce. In this way the Boeotians gained possession of Oenoe, and the oligarchy and the troubles at Athens ended.

To return to the Peloponnesians at Miletus. No pay was forthcoming from any of the agents Tissaphernes had deputed for that purpose on his departure for Aspendus. Neither the Phoenician fleet nor Tissaphernes himself showed any sign of appearing, and Philip, who had been sent with him, and another Spartan, Hippocrates, who was at Phaselis, wrote word to Mindarus, the admiral, that the ships were not coming at all, and that they were being grossly cheated by Tissaphernes. Meanwhile Pharnabazus was inviting them to come, and was making every effort to get the fleet, and like Tissaphernes, to bring about the revolt of the cities in his government still subject to Athens, founding great hopes on his success. At length, around the period of the summer we have now reached, Mindarus yielded to his importunities, and, with great order and at a moment's notice, in order to elude the enemy at Samos, weighed anchor with seventy-three ships from Miletus and set sail for the Hellespont. Sixteen vessels had already preceded him there in the same summer and had overrun part of the Chersonese. Caught in a storm, Mindarus was forced to put in at Icarus, and after being detained five or six days there by stress of weather, arrived at Chios.

Meanwhile Thrasyllus had heard that he had put out from Miletus, and immediately set sail with fifty-five ships from Samos, in haste to arrive in the Hellespont before him. Learning that he was at Chios and expecting that he would stay there, he posted scouts in Lesbos and on the continent opposite to prevent the fleet moving without his knowing it, and himself coasted along to Methymna and gave orders to prepare meal and other necessaries, in order to attack them from Lesbos in the event of their staying any length of time at Chios. Meanwhile he resolved to sail against Eresus, a town in Lesbos that had revolted, and, if he could, to take it. For some of the principal Methymnian exiles had carried over about fifty heavy infantry, their sworn associates, from Cuma, and hiring others from the continent, so as to make up three hundred in all, chose Anaxander, a Theban, to command them, on account of the kinship between the Thebans and the Lesbians, and first attacked Methymna. Balked in this attempt by the advance of the Athenian guards from Mitylene, and repulsed a second time in a battle outside the city, they then crossed the mountain and brought about the revolt of Eresus. Thrasyllus accordingly determined to go there with all his ships and to attack the place. Meanwhile Thrasybulus had preceded him there with five ships from Samos, as soon as he heard the exiles had crossed over, and coming too late to save Eresus, went on and anchored before the town. Here they were also joined by two vessels on their way home from the Hellespont, and by the ships of the Methymnians, making a grand total of sixty-seven vessels. The forces on board now made ready with engines and every other available means to do their utmost to storm Eresus.

In the meantime Mindarus and the Peloponnesian fleet at Chios, after taking provisions for two days and receiving three Chian pieces of money for each man from the Chians, on the third day put out in haste from the island. To avoid falling in with the ships at Eresus, they did not make for the open sea, but keeping Lesbos on their left, sailed for the continent. After touching at the port of Carteria, in the Phocaeid, and dining, they went on along the Cumaean coast and supped at Arginusae, on the continent opposite Mitylene. From there they continued their voyage along the coast, although it was late in the night, and arriving at Harmatus on the continent opposite Methymna, dined there. Swiftly passing Lectum, Larisa, Hamaxitus, and the neighboring towns, they arrived a little before midnight at Rhoeteum. Here they were now in the Hellespont. Some of the ships also put in at Sigeum and at other places nearby.

Meanwhile the warnings of the fire signals and the sudden increase in the number of fires on the enemy's shore informed the eighteen Athenian ships at Sestos of the approach of the Peloponnesian fleet. That very night they set sail in haste just as they were, and hugging the shore of the Chersonese, coasted along to Elaeus, in order to sail out into the open sea, away from the enemy's fleet.

After passing unobserved the sixteen ships at Abydos — which had nevertheless been warned by their approaching friends to be on the alert to prevent their sailing out — at dawn they sighted the fleet of Mindarus, which immediately gave chase. They had not all time to get away. The greater number, however, escaped to Imbros and Lemnos, while four of the hindmost were overtaken off Elaeus. One of these was stranded opposite the temple of Protesilaus and taken with its crew, two others without their crews; the fourth was abandoned on the shore of Imbros and burned by the enemy.

After this the Peloponnesians were joined by the squadron from Abydos, which made up their fleet to a grand total of eighty-six vessels. They spent the day unsuccessfully besieging Elaeus, and then sailed back to Abydos. Meanwhile the Athenians, deceived by their scouts, and never imagining that the enemy's fleet had got by undetected, were tranquilly besieging Eresus. As soon as they heard the news they instantly abandoned Eresus and made with all speed for the Hellespont. After taking two of the Peloponnesian ships that had been carried out too far into the open sea in the ardor of the pursuit and now fell in their way, the next day they dropped anchor at Elaeus. Bringing back the ships that had taken refuge at Imbros, they spent five days preparing for the coming engagement.

After this they engaged in the following way. The Athenians formed in column and sailed close alongshore to Sestos. On seeing this, the Peloponnesians put out from Abydos to meet them. Realizing that a battle was now imminent, both sides extended their flank: the Athenians along the Chersonese from Idacus to Arrhiani with seventy-six ships, the Peloponnesians from Abydos to Dardanus with eighty-six. The Peloponnesian right wing was held by the Syracusans, their left by Mindarus in person with the best sailers in the navy. The Athenian left was held by Thrasyllus, their right by Thrasybulus, the other commanders being in different parts of the fleet. The Peloponnesians hastened to engage first, and outflanking with their left the Athenian right, sought to cut them off, if possible, from sailing out of the straits, and to drive their center onto the shore, which was not far off. The Athenians, perceiving their intention, extended their own wing and outsailed them, while their left had by this time passed the point of Cynossema. This, however, obliged them to thin and weaken their center, especially as they had fewer ships than the enemy, and as the coast around Point Cynossema formed a sharp angle that prevented them from seeing what was happening on the other side of it.

The Peloponnesians now attacked their center and drove the Athenian ships ashore, and disembarked to follow up their victory. No help could be given to the center either by the squadron of Thrasybulus on the right, owing to the number of ships attacking him, or by that of Thrasyllus on the left, from whom the point of Cynossema hid what was going on, and who was also held up by his Syracusan and other opponents, whose numbers were fully equal to his own. At length, however, the Peloponnesians, in the confidence of victory, began to scatter in pursuit of the enemy's ships, and allowed a considerable part of their fleet to get into disorder. On seeing this, the squadron of Thrasybulus discontinued their lateral movement and, facing about, attacked and routed the ships opposed to them. They next fell harshly on the scattered vessels of the victorious Peloponnesian division, and put most of them to flight without a blow. The Syracusans also had by this time given way before the squadron of Thrasyllus, and now openly took to flight on seeing the flight of their comrades.

The rout was now complete. Most of the Peloponnesians fled for refuge first to the river Midius and afterwards to Abydos. Only a few ships were taken by the Athenians, since owing to the narrowness of the Hellespont the enemy had not far to go to reach safety. Nevertheless nothing could have been more opportune for them than this victory. Up to this time they had feared the Peloponnesian fleet, owing to a number of petty losses and to the disaster in Sicily. But they now ceased to mistrust themselves, or any longer to think their enemies good for anything at sea. Meanwhile they took from the enemy eight Chian vessels, five Corinthian, two Ambraciot, two Boeotian, and one each Leucadian, Lacedaemonian, Syracusan, and Pellenian, losing fifteen of their own. After setting up a trophy on Point Cynossema, securing the wrecks, and giving back the enemy's dead under truce, they sent off a galley to Athens with the news of their victory. The arrival of this vessel with its unhoped-for good news, after the recent disasters in Euboea and during the revolution at Athens, gave fresh courage to the Athenians, and made them believe that if they put their shoulders to the wheel, their cause might yet prevail.

On the fourth day after the sea-fight, the Athenians at Sestos, having hastily refitted their ships, sailed against Cyzicus, which had revolted. Off Harpagium and Priapus they sighted at anchor the eight vessels from Byzantium, and sailing up and routing the troops on shore, took the ships, and then went on and recovered the town of Cyzicus, which was unfortified, and levied money from the citizens. Meanwhile the Peloponnesians sailed from Abydos to Elaeus and recovered such of their captured galleys as were still uninjured, the rest having been burned by the Elaeusians, and sent Hippocrates and Epicles to Euboea to fetch the squadron from that island.

About the same time Alcibiades returned with his thirteen ships from Caunus and Phaselis to Samos, bringing word that he had prevented the Phoenician fleet from joining the Peloponnesians, and had made Tissaphernes more friendly to the Athenians than before. Alcibiades now manned nine more ships, levied large sums of money from the Halicarnassians, and fortified Cos. After doing this and placing a governor in Cos, he sailed back to Samos, autumn being now at hand. Meanwhile Tissaphernes, on hearing that the Peloponnesian fleet had sailed from Miletus to the Hellespont, set off back again from Aspendus, and made all sail for Ionia. While the Peloponnesians were in the Hellespont, the Antandrians, a people of Aeolic extraction, conveyed by land across Mount Ida some heavy infantry from Abydos, and introduced them into the town. They had been ill-treated by Arsaces, the Persian lieutenant of Tissaphernes. This same Arsaces had, on the pretext of a secret quarrel, invited the chief men of the Delians to undertake military service (these were Delians who had settled at Atramyttium after having been driven from their homes by the Athenians for the sake of purifying Delos). After drawing them out of their town as his friends and allies, he had laid an ambush for them at dinner, and surrounded them and had them shot down by his soldiers. This deed made the Antandrians fear that he might some day do them harm. As he was also laying on them burdens too heavy for them to bear, they expelled his garrison from their citadel.

Tissaphernes, on hearing of this act of the Peloponnesians, in addition to what had happened at Miletus and Cnidus, where his garrisons had also been expelled, now saw that the breach between them was serious. Fearing further injury from them, and also vexed to think that Pharnabazus should receive them, and in less time and at less cost perhaps succeed better against Athens than he himself had done, he determined to rejoin them in the Hellespont, in order to complain of the events at Antandros and excuse himself as best he could on the matter of the Phoenician fleet and of the other charges against him. Accordingly he went first to Ephesus and offered sacrifice to Artemis....
[When the winter after this summer is over, the twenty-first year of this war will be completed.]
